name: Merck stitch otoplasty

lead: The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive ear-pinning method. Sutures are placed through small puncture incisions instead of an open cut behind the ear, reshaping the ear without cutting cartilage so it sits closer to the head.

It was published in 2013 and sits within the suture-only group of otoplasty techniques, contrasted with Mustardé's open approach and larger incision. Sources describing it are sparse and no technique-specific studies were found.

paras: A surgeon passes sutures through stab incisions to fold and hold the cartilage in its new shape. Because it is closed, there is no long incision behind the ear.
General suture-otoplasty risks include suture extrusion, hematoma, infection and recurrence. No technique-specific figures were found.

angle.text: Stitches placed through tiny stab incisions reshape the ear without a long cut or cartilage cutting, setting it closer to the head. The pinned-back ear is visible after healing. It was published in 2013, and outcome data are sparse.

lead: The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive ear-pinning (otoplasty) method in which permanent sutures are placed through small stab incisions in the groove behind the ear to pull prominent ears closer to the head, without cutting the cartilage. People choose it to bring protruding ears into proportion with a shorter, less invasive procedure than an open operation.[1]

W. H. Merck reportedly developed the technique in 1995, began using it on patients in 1996 and described it in a 2013 publication. He reports that it works without cartilage scoring or cutting and cites several thousand operated ears, though these claims are not independently verified in the source.[1] It falls within the suture-only group of otoplasty techniques and is contrasted with Mustarde's open approach, which exposes the cartilage and removes skin.[2]
No published clinical studies of the Merck stitch itself were found; its reported results rest largely on Merck's own description.[1]

paras: The surgeon makes small stab incisions in the groove behind the ear. Permanent, non-absorbable sutures are placed under the skin around the antihelix cartilage, tightened and knotted, which draws the ear closer to the head. The cartilage is not cut or reshaped. A protruding earlobe can also be pinned back if the cartilage extends into it.[1]

Wikipedia contrasts this with Mustarde's open method, in which the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, some skin is removed and mattress sutures define the antihelical fold, and says Merck stitch patients generally do not need a dressing.[2]

Fritsch, an earlier user, combined the method with the Furnas technique and later argued that lasting results required cutting the cartilage; Merck disputes this.[1] Other approaches include Stenstrom cartilage scoring and the Fritsch method, which combines minimally invasive suturing with scoring.[2]

Possible problems include pain, suture extrusion, infection, rare suture granuloma, slight postoperative bleeding and relapse, in which the ear protrudes again.[1] For otoplasty generally, Wikipedia lists suture extrusion behind the ear as the most common complication, with overcorrection and unnatural contours considered the most significant.[2]
No studies found on the Merck stitch itself. Studies of related closed otoplasty techniques exist, such as percutaneous adjustable closed otoplasty, but are separate procedures.

timeline.event: Merck reportedly develops the technique and starts using it on patients.[1]
